newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan's Mr Yen reaches top financial diplomat post.
newsitem.headline: Japan's Mr Yen reaches top financial diplomat post.

text.p: Eisuke Sakakibara, the outspoken Finance Ministry official dubbed "Mr Yen" for his influence over currency markets, became Tokyo's top financial diplomat on Tuesday and vowed to maintain his vigilance over the markets.

"When the market is in a frenzy for no legitimate reason, one of our important tasks is to communicate correct information," Sakakibara told his first news conference as Japan's vice minister for international affairs.

He also downplayed the recent turmoil engulfing Thailand's baht and other Southeast Asian currencies, declaring that there is no crisis while promising that Japan would cooperate where it can to address the region's currency woes.

During his two years heading the ministry's international finance bureau, Sakakibara played a key role in forging pacts with Asian nations to stabilise regional currencies, and one of his first tasks in his new job will be to restore calm to the markets.
Sakakibara's promotion to vice finance minister was both a vindication of his controversial style and a reward for spearheading a successful drive to counter the yen's steep rise in 1995.
The currency's appreciation dealt a severe blow to Japan's exporters and threatened to put its economy in disarray.

In addition to pulling down the yen to its current level of more than 110 yen to the dollar, from a post-war high of about 79 yen in April 1995, Sakakibara has been instrumental in revising Japan's foreign exchange laws as a step towards Tokyo's "Big Bang" financial reforms.
But reaching the pinnacle of Japan's international finance hierarchy was not easy.
Sakakibara's aggressive personality and alleged missteps in the past won him many enemies within the ministry.
He once considered seeking a career in politics and such bold ambitions were not welcomed among his colleagues at the conservative ministry.
But the tide appears to have shifted since then.

"His support in the ministry is much more broad-based than two years ago. Then, he was odd man out for his controversial views and controversial ways of doing things. But success has proven him right," said Jesper Koll, chief economist at JP Morgan.

"He's someone you can depend on. He's always firmly in control and knows what to do in order to achieve a certain goal," added a ministry official who worked under him in revising the foreign exchange laws.

A fluent English speaker who earned a doctorate at the University of Michigan after graduating from the prestigious University of Tokyo, Sakakibara's economic views also earned him a place among a circle of intellectuals and bureaucrats dubbed by some as Japan's new nationalists.

Those views were laid out in his book "Beyond Capitalism", in which he argued that Japan has a distinctive non-capitalist market economy which might be a better guide for developing nations than the U.S. model. Japanese firms, he said, compete in more or less free markets but the system places people above profits and mere efficiency.
Sakakibara showed that even his appointment to the powerful vice minister's post had not changed the "nationalist" in him.

"It's time that we clearly lay out what Japan's intentions are. To stress one's views does not necessarily put a strain on relationships. What is the national interest of Japan? What is its identity? We should make them clear," he said.
